problem_framing.reason: A1 separates the objective from the suggested solution and lists real alternatives, including a channel-only change and no expansion. Two problems keep the score low. First, the €20,000 / 12-week budget is stated as a constraint, but the case does not supply it, so it is unsupported (the rubric caps this at 1). Second, A1 says 'indirect channels are unknown', which contradicts mettler-ar25-channels: less complicated products go through indirect channels. A1 also misses the Ohaus lower-cost route (mettler-ar25-ohaus), an obvious existing vehicle.

causal_mechanism.reason: T1 names a benefit (accurate carbohydrate counting) and a user group. It never explains why a Mettler scale would be preferred, since the NHS source says any 'digital kitchen scales' help. The behaviour driver ('growing awareness') is asserted without evidence. The value-capture step, a premium scale sold through the direct sales force, conflicts with the channel source. It also assumes an untested 'carbohydrate measurement feature' that a weighing source does not describe.

distinct_theories.reason: T1 (carbohydrate accuracy for diabetics) and T2 (convenience for busy households) are rival motives with different target customers. Both share the same product category, channel and value-capture story. No theory considers that consumer entry fails, or that value lies in Ohaus or indirect channels.

assumptions_predictions.reason: The predictions are observable: purchase intent at least 20% higher, and the primary reason customers cite. The 20% threshold is an arbitrary assumption. Some assumptions are vague, such as 'awareness ... growing'. The T1 predictions concern a feature, not willingness to pay at a premium, so failing them would not clearly threaten the premium value-capture claim.

evidence_judgement.reason: A11 states what the NHS source does not show, which is useful. However, A11 labels the source 'independent_study' when the dossier class is verified_observation. A12 calls the channel source neutral when it actually cuts against the direct-sales route recommended in A15/A16. Several relevant sources are never assessed: mettler-techgearlab-small-loads (precision differentiation), mettler-dcn-acaia (an existing funded competitor), mettler-ar25-ohaus and mettler-atk-by-weight. There is no discussion of date, place or customer-group fit.

seeking_challenge.reason: A13 runs one search against T1 but never reports or assesses what it found. The competitor evidence (mettler-dcn-acaia, surfaced in A5) and the channel contradiction are never engaged as challenges.

experiment_design.reason: The predictions do not separate the theories. In a binary choice, 'at least 20% choose A' (T1) and 'at least 20% choose standard' (T2) can both hold at once, for example at a 50/50 split. The test includes no convenience or speed attribute, so choosing the standard scale says nothing about T2. There is no price attribute, so it cannot measure the willingness to pay that A16 says it will resolve. The cost, sample and thresholds are unvalidated assumptions.

revision.reason: Revision is excluded from packet.applicable_dimensions, and no update was scheduled.

recommendation.reason: A16 recommends investing before any demand or willingness-to-pay evidence exists, while rating T1 'likely' on the basis of a single health-advice excerpt. Its claim that the test 'will resolve' willingness to pay is false given the test design. Its reversal condition (standard chosen by at least 20%, read as 'strong demand for convenience') is an unsound inference. It names a next action but is not supported by the evidence.

red_flags.reason: The T1 and T2 predictions can both be satisfied at the same time. The test has no convenience attribute and no price attribute, so it cannot separate the theories or measure willingness to pay.

The plan to sell a consumer kitchen scale through the direct sales force at a premium contradicts mettler-ar25-channels, which says less complicated products go indirect. Premium pricing and brand leverage among consumers have no supporting source.
The NHS excerpt supports weighing food with any digital scale. It does not support demand for a differentiated or premium Mettler product, yet T1 is rated 'likely' and investment is recommended.
A1 states 'indirect channels are unknown' despite a source describing indirect channels. It also introduces a test budget and timeline that the case does not provide.
The source class is mislabelled: mettler-nhs-carb-counting is given as independent_study, but the dossier says verified_observation.

The searches report source IDs that are absent from the dossier (mettler-atk-tolerance, mettler-atk-certified-rival, mettler-q3-2026-sales, mettler-atk-precision-winner) and cannot be verified. They were not used in any assessment.
The reversal condition maps 'standard chosen by at least 20%' to convenience demand. That is an unsound decision mapping given the test design.

judgment.screen_reason: Rejected. The episode is complete but contains material errors: a non-discriminating test (A14), unsupported inferences about premium pricing and the direct-sales route that contradict the channel source (A15/A16), a recommendation to invest that the evidence does not support, and an unsound reversal rule. Scored under automated evaluation only.
